items.title: Judaism centres on covenant — a binding agreement with God
items.claim: What is the relationship between the Abrahamic and Mosaic covenants in Judaism?

options.text: The Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17, sealed by circumcision) promises land and descendants; the Mosaic covenant (Exodus 19-24, at Sinai) gives the Torah law — both remain binding on Jews
There is only one covenant — at Sinai
Covenants applied only to ancient Israelites, not modern Jews

items.reveal:
Brit milah (covenant of circumcision) is performed on Jewish boys on the eighth day after birth, marking the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:11-13). The Mosaic covenant at Sinai (around 1300 BCE in traditional dating) establishes the 613 mitzvot (commandments) of the Torah law.

The Noahide covenant (Genesis 9) — applying to all humanity — is also recognised. Rabbinic Judaism distinguishes seven Noahide laws binding on all people from the 613 mitzvot binding specifically on Jews.

Christianity reinterprets these covenants through 'new covenant' theology (Hebrews 8); Judaism rejects supersessionism — the older covenants are not abrogated.
items.why: Covenant is not a vague concept of relationship. In Judaism it is a specific structure with terms, obligations and consequences — and a major point of theological disagreement with Christianity.

items.title: Aquinas offered Five Ways, not one argument

options.text: Five distinct a posteriori arguments in Summa Theologiae I.2.3: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer)

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes a priori arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from a posteriori arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move; an unmoved mover is required. Second Way (efficient causation): a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised separately. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's exchange with Copleston (1948 BBC debate) challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.

items.title: Aristotle reached medieval Europe via Arabic translations
items.claim: Most of Aristotle's works were lost to Latin Europe by 500 CE. How did Aquinas (d. 1274) have access to them?

options.text: They had been continuously preserved in Vatican archives
Via Arabic translations and commentaries by Muslim scholars like Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Averroes (Ibn Rushd), re-translated into Latin in the 12th-13th centuries
Marco Polo brought them back from China
They were rediscovered in Constantinople after 1453

items.reveal:
From the 8th-10th centuries, the Abbasid Caliphate's 'House of Wisdom' (Bayt al-Hikma) in Baghdad sponsored translation of Greek philosophy and science into Arabic. Ibn Sina (Avicenna, d. 1037) and Ibn Rushd (Averroes, d. 1198) wrote major commentaries.

In 12th-century Toledo and Sicily, Christian, Jewish and Muslim scholars translated these Arabic texts into Latin. Aquinas's engagement with Aristotle relies heavily on Averroes (the 'Commentator'). Without that chain, scholastic philosophy as we know it would not exist.
items.why: Histories of European thought often skip the Islamic intermediary entirely. The intellectual map of medieval Europe makes no sense without it.
